body_markdown:
Run a baseline properly and the first thing it produces isn’t a clean record. It’s a list of everything that didn’t match: the site marked active that’s actually decommissioned, the lease that renewed months ago but never made it into the program’s system, the equipment count that’s been wrong since before this program existed.


That list is uncomfortable to look at. It’s also the reason a baseline is worth doing properly, rather than fast.


### What You’re Really Building


Most programs treat the baseline as a deliverable: a picture of the estate, signed off and filed, ready to build a schedule and budget on top of. That misses what the work actually requires. Getting to a record worth building on means finding every place the old one was wrong and resolving it, not noting it and moving past it.


The record is the output everyone expects. The discrepancies are the work that has to happen before it’s trustworthy. Skip past them and the record looks finished without being right.


### The shortcut that costs more later


Under schedule pressure, it’s tempting to treat “a starting point” as good enough – take whatever picture is closest to hand, note the gaps, and assume it’ll get sorted out along the way. It rarely does. A baseline with known gaps doesn’t get quieter over time. It gets built on top of, by a schedule and budget that assume it’s correct, until the gap surfaces as a missed deadline or a number that doesn’t reconcile at reporting time.


Properly baselining means resolving discrepancies before the program treats the record as settled. Later rarely comes.


### What’s actually at stake


A wrong baseline isn’t an internal inconvenience. It’s the foundation everything else gets built on. Crews get allocated to sites that turn out not to be ready, because the resourcing plan was built against an inaccurate picture. Overruns follow naturally: a budget built on a wrong baseline is wrong from day one, and the gap between planned and actual cost grows as the program discovers, site by site, what the record didn’t tell it. Timelines slip for the same reason.


A program that starts on a strong foundation, resources allocated correctly, budget and schedule built on numbers that hold up, has a real chance of staying on track. A program that starts on a weak one is absorbing risk it won’t see the full cost of until much later.


The cost isn’t fixed, either. The longer an error sits uncaught, and the further down the delivery chain it’s found, the more it costs to fix. Caught at the baseline, it’s a correction. Caught after crews are scheduled, it’s a re-plan. Caught after contractors are mobilized, it’s rework and renegotiation. Caught at handover or in front of a customer, it’s a missed commitment nobody can quietly absorb. The error doesn’t change. What it costs to fix multiplies at every stage it survives.


### Why this feels uncomfortable


A list of discrepancies reads like a list of mistakes, and it’s tempting to treat it that way. Nobody wants to be the one whose system was three sites behind. So the instinct is to smooth the list over quickly and move on.


That instinct is exactly what turns a proper baseline into a rough one. Each discrepancy is evidence of where and how the estate record drifts. Working through the list properly, rather than around it, is what makes the baseline something the program can rely on.


### Getting it right isn’t a one-time event


A baseline done properly still won’t stay accurate on its own. Leasing, network, and ops keep updating on their own schedules, and drift starts again the moment the baseline is signed off. Programs that avoid repeating this exercise from zero are the ones that keep the record current afterward – the same discipline that built it, applied continuously rather than once.


That’s the difference between a baseline as a one-time cleanup and a baseline as a standard the program holds itself to.
